# 12. The limits: diffraction, resolution and seeing

*Why can't a telescope just keep magnifying until it shows a rover on Mars? Two things stop it. Light is a wave, so
it spreads as it passes through any opening and even a perfect telescope turns a star into a tiny disc with rings.
And the air above us is always stirring, which blurs every picture taken from the ground. This chapter explains both
limits, how astronomers measure them, the high, dry places where the air is steadiest, and the tricks used to beat the
blur: fast cameras, mirrors that change shape to follow the air, telescopes in space and telescopes joined
together. It asks how much detail we can see on Mars from Earth, from orbit and from Mars itself.*

!!! abstract "In this chapter"
    **You will learn:**

    - why even a perfect telescope cannot make a point image of a star
    - what the Airy disc is, and why a bigger telescope makes it smaller
    - when two stars can be told apart
    - what seeing is, and why stars twinkle but planets mostly do not
    - where the steadiest air on Earth is
    - how speckle imaging, lucky imaging and adaptive optics beat the blur
    - what went wrong with Hubble's mirror
    - how telescopes far apart can work together
    - how much detail can be seen on Mars from Earth, from orbit and from Mars
    - where the number 1.22 comes from

    **You need:** chapters 1 (waves and Young's two slits), 9, 10 and 11. The physics lesson
    [Seeing Earth from Mars](https://physics.akadian.ca/topics/waves/level-7/06-seeing-earth-from-mars.html) helps.

    **Levels:** 12.1 to 12.3 are beginner; 12.4 to 12.9 are intermediate; 12.10 is advanced; 12.11 is expert.

## 12.1 Light spreads out { #spread }

Stand round a corner from a radio and you can still hear it. Sound waves bend around the corner and spread out after
passing through a doorway. Ripples on water do the same as they pass through a gap. This spreading of waves past an
edge or through an opening is called **diffraction**.

Light is a wave too (chapter 1), so it diffracts, but its waves are so short, about half a millionth of a metre,
that the spreading is tiny and easy to miss.

- **Bologna, 1660.** The Italian Jesuit priest **Francesco Maria Grimaldi**, who taught at the Jesuit college in
  Bologna, made the first careful observations of it. He named it from the Latin *diffringere*, "to break into
  pieces", for the way light seemed to break up as it passed an edge. His book came out in 1665, two years after he
  died. A crater on the Moon is named after him.
- **England, 1800.** **Thomas Young** gave the first explanation of diffraction using waves.
- **France, from 1817.** Augustin-Jean Fresnel's wave theory, and the bright spot that François Arago found in the
  middle of a round shadow, settled the matter (chapter 1,
  [section 1.5](01-What-Light-Is.md#young)).

**The rule.** The narrower the opening compared with the wavelength, the more the wave spreads. A telescope's aperture
is an opening, so it too spreads the light that passes through it, by an angle of about the wavelength divided by the
aperture.

??? note "Sources"
    - Grimaldi's careful observations, published after his death in 1665, the word from *diffringere*, and Young's
      first wave treatment of diffraction in 1800: Wikipedia, [Diffraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffraction)
      (weaker).
    - Grimaldi as a Jesuit who taught at the Jesuit college in Bologna, 1618 to 1663, and the crater named after him:
      Wikipedia, [Francesco Maria Grimaldi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Maria_Grimaldi) (weaker).
    - Fresnel and Arago: chapter 1, section 1.5.

## 12.2 The image of a star { #airy }

A star is so far away that it is, for any telescope, a point. Chapter 11 said a lens brings the light of a point back
to a point. Diffraction says it cannot quite. The best a perfect telescope can do is a small bright disc surrounded by
faint rings, called the **Airy pattern**; the disc in the middle is the **Airy disc**.

*Figure A. The image of a star in a perfect telescope, and its brightness across the middle.*

- **1828.** John Herschel described the disc and rings seen around a bright star at high magnification.
- **1835.** **George Biddell Airy** worked out the full theory of the pattern made
  by a round lens.

The first dark ring lies at an angle

$$\theta = 1.22\,\frac{\lambda}{D}$$

from the centre, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength and $D$ the aperture, with $\theta$ in radians. Double the aperture
and the disc shrinks to half the size. Red light, with its longer waves, makes a bigger disc than blue.

??? note "Sources"
    - The Airy disc and pattern as the best-focused spot a perfect lens with a circular aperture can make, Airy's
      paper of 1835, Herschel's description of 1828, and the first dark ring at $\sin\theta \approx 1.22\lambda/d$:
      Wikipedia, [Airy disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airy_disk) (weaker).
    - The figure is ours, drawn from the formula in section 12.11.

## 12.3 Telling two stars apart { #rayleigh }

Two stars close together make two Airy patterns that overlap. When can you still see that there are two?

<div class="pattern-row" markdown="0">
<svg viewBox="0 0 340 250" role="img" aria-label="Three graphs of the brightness of two equal stars seen side by side, each star making an Airy pattern. Left: the stars are two units apart, measured in units of the wavelength divided by the aperture, and show as two clear peaks. Middle: they are 1.22 units apart, so the peak of each star falls on the first dark ring of the other; there is a small dip between the peaks, and the stars are just resolved. This is the Rayleigh criterion. Right: they are 0.6 units apart and blend into a single hump; they cannot be told apart.">

    <text x="280.0" y="216" text-anchor="middle">0.6 λ/D apart</text>
    <text x="6" y="12">Two equal stars: when can you tell them apart?</text>
    <text x="6" y="240">dashed: each star alone; solid: what you see</text>
  </g>
</svg>
</div>

*Figure B. Two equal stars at three separations, measured in units of $\lambda/D$.*

- **Rayleigh's rule, 1879.** **Lord Rayleigh** (chapter 3) suggested that two points are just separated, or
  **resolved**, when the centre of one falls on the first dark ring of the other: an angle of $1.22\lambda/D$. In
  figure B there is then a clear dip between the two peaks.
- **Dawes' limit, 1867.** Earlier, **William Rutter Dawes** had tested real observers on pairs of
  equal stars. He found that a telescope of aperture $D$ millimetres can split pairs down to about $116/D$ seconds of
  arc. That matches Rayleigh's rule for blue light of about 460 nm.

So a 100 mm telescope can split stars 1.2 to 1.4″ apart, and a 200 mm telescope stars half as far apart.

**Your eye.** With a 7 mm pupil, diffraction would allow about 20″. In fact good eyesight, called 20/20 or 6/6,
separates lines 1.75 mm apart at 6 m, about 1′, three times coarser. The eye's own lens is not perfect, and the
light-sensing cone cells of the retina (book 1, [chapter 1](../night-sky/01-Your-First-Clear-Night.md)) are only so
closely packed. Only when the pupil is very small, 1 to 2 mm, does diffraction set the limit.

??? note "Sources"
    - The Rayleigh criterion, the principal maximum of one falling on the first minimum of the other, $1.22\lambda/D$,
      Rayleigh's paper of 1879, and Dawes' tests of human observers on close equal pairs: Wikipedia,
      [Angular resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_resolution) (weaker).
    - Dawes' limit, $R = 116/D$ with $D$ in millimetres, his catalogue of 1867, and agreement with $1.22\lambda/D$
      at about 460 nm: Wikipedia, [Dawes' limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawes%27_limit) (weaker).
    - 6/6 vision separating contours about 1.75 mm apart at 6 m, the optics of the eye and the density of cones in
      the fovea, and diffraction limiting sharpness only for a pupil of 1 to 2 mm: Wikipedia,
      [Visual acuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_acuity) (weaker).
    - The arithmetic is ours.

## 12.4 Seeing { #seeing }

From the ground, diffraction is rarely the real limit. The air is.

Layers of air at different temperatures, moving at different speeds, bend light by slightly different amounts
(chapter 10). They act like weak, shifting lenses and prisms. Astronomers call the blurring that results **seeing**.

- **Twinkling.** To the eye, seeing makes stars flicker in brightness, colour and position (book 1,
  [chapter 4, section 4.4](../night-sky/04-How-Bright-Is-a-Star.md#limit)). Planets usually do not flicker much: they
  are small discs, not points, and the light from different parts of the disc wobbles in different ways and averages
  out.
- **In a telescope.** At high magnification the image of a star breaks up into a cluster of dancing specks that
  change many times a second. In a longer exposure they smear into a blob, the **seeing disc**.
- **How good is it?** Seeing is given as the width of that blob. A seeing disc smaller than 0.4″ is excellent. Before
  Hubble, ground telescopes were held to about 0.5 to 1″ however large they were.

So a 200 mm telescope, whose diffraction limit is 0.7″, can use nearly all its aperture on a good night. A 10 m
telescope, whose limit is 0.014″, cannot: in ordinary seeing it shows hardly any finer detail than the 200 mm one. It
still collects 2,500 times more light, so it reaches much fainter stars.

??? note "Sources"
    - Seeing as turbulence in the Earth's atmosphere, layers of different temperature and wind speed, visible as
      blurring, twinkling or distortion, stars breaking up into rapidly changing speckle patterns, the seeing disc,
      and below 0.4″ as excellent: Wikipedia, [Astronomical seeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_seeing)
      (weaker).
    - Turbulence acting like lenses and prisms, stars as points and planets as resolved discs whose light averages
      out, so planets flicker less: Wikipedia,
      [Twinkling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twinkling) (weaker).
    - Ground-based telescopes limited to 0.5 to 1.0″: Wikipedia,
      [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope) (weaker).
    - The arithmetic is ours.

## 12.5 Where the air is steadiest { #sites }

Astronomers go high, to get above as much air as possible, and to places where the air flows smoothly.

- **Islands.** The best seeing is usually found at high observatories on small islands, such as **Mauna Kea** in
  Hawaii and **La Palma** in the Canary Islands.
- **The Himalayas.** India's **Indian Astronomical Observatory** at **Hanle** in Ladakh stands at 4,500 m, one of the
  highest sites in the world for optical, infrared and gamma-ray telescopes. Its 2 m **Himalayan Chandra Telescope**
  is named after the India-born Nobel prize winner Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar.
- **Antarctica.** **Dome C**, a high point of the Antarctic ice sheet at 3,233 m, also called Dôme Concordia, was
  tested with weather balloons. About 87% of the turbulence turned out to lie in the lowest 36 m. A telescope on a
  tower above that layer could have excellent seeing.

The observatories of the world, and why so many are on mountaintops, return in chapter 16.

??? note "Sources"
    - The best conditions at high observatories on small islands such as Mauna Kea and La Palma: Wikipedia,
      [Astronomical seeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_seeing) (weaker).
    - Hanle at 4,500 m, among the world's highest sites, and the 2.01 m Himalayan Chandra Telescope named after
      Chandrasekhar: Wikipedia,
      [Indian Astronomical Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Astronomical_Observatory) (weaker).
    - Dome C at 3,233 m, Concordia, 87% of the turbulence below 36 m, and a tower above the boundary layer: Wikipedia,
      [Dome C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dome_C) (weaker).

## 12.6 Beating the blur { #tricks }

**Freeze it.** In 1970 the French astronomer **Antoine Labeyrie** showed that many very short exposures, each freezing
the dancing specks, hold the fine detail that a long exposure loses. Working it out from their patterns is called
**speckle interferometry**. In the early 1970s photographic film caught only about 7% of the light, so only the
brightest objects could be studied; modern cameras (chapter 14) do far better.

**Pick the best.** **Lucky imaging** takes many pictures of a tenth of a second or less, keeps the sharpest, typically
about 10%, and adds them together. Amateur astronomers use it as well as professionals.

**Bend the mirror.** **Adaptive optics** measures how the air has bent the light and undoes it, using:

- a **wavefront sensor**, which takes some of the light and measures the distortion;
- a **deformable mirror**, whose surface can change shape;
- a fast computer, which links the two.

The American astronomer **Horace Babcock** proposed the idea in 1953. Some early work was done by the US military in
the Cold War, to track Soviet satellites, and it came into common use only in the 1990s, when computers became fast
enough. Today an 8 to 10 m telescope such as Keck can reach 0.03 to 0.06″ in the infrared, against about 1″ without
it.

**Make a star.** Adaptive optics needs a fairly bright star near the target to measure the air. Where there is none,
a laser makes one. Tuned to 589 nm, the yellow sodium line (chapter 7), it lights up a layer of sodium atoms about
90 km up, and that glowing spot serves as an artificial **guide star**.

??? note "Sources"
    - Labeyrie's speckle interferometry of 1970, and film capturing only about 7% of the light in the early 1970s:
      Wikipedia, [Speckle imaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speckle_imaging) (weaker).
    - Lucky imaging, exposures of 100 ms or less, about 10% kept, used by amateurs and professionals: Wikipedia,
      [Lucky imaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucky_imaging) (weaker).
    - Wavefront sensor, deformable mirror and computer, Babcock in 1953, the US military, the 1990s, and 30 to 60
      milliarcseconds for 8 to 10 m telescopes in the infrared against about 1″: Wikipedia,
      [Adaptive optics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptive_optics) (weaker).
    - Sodium beacons at 589.2 nm in the sodium layer about 90 km up: Wikipedia,
      [Laser guide star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_guide_star) (weaker).

## 12.7 Above the air, and a mistake of 2 micrometres { #hubble }

The surest way to escape seeing is to leave the air behind. NASA and ESA's **Hubble Space Telescope**, launched in
1990 with a 2.4 m mirror, was meant to reach its diffraction limit of about 0.05″, ten or twenty times sharper than
the ground (history book, [chapter 22, section 22.2](../history/22-Astronomy-Today.md#space)).

Its first pictures were blurred. Hubble's mirror was among the smoothest ever made, but its outer edge was too flat by
about 2,200 nanometres, roughly a 450th of a millimetre. That was enough to give it bad **spherical aberration**
(chapter 9): light from the edge of the mirror focused in a different place from light from the middle. An inquiry
found that a testing device used to check the mirror's shape had been put together wrongly.

In 1993, astronauts on the Space Shuttle mission STS-61 fitted corrective optics, rather like glasses, and
Hubble at last saw as sharply as planned.

??? note "Sources"
    - Launch in 1990, the mirror ground incorrectly, smooth to about 10 nm but too flat at the edge by about 2,200 nm,
      spherical aberration, the null corrector incorrectly assembled, correction by STS-61 in 1993, and the
      theoretical 0.05″ against 0.5 to 1.0″ on the ground: Wikipedia,
      [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope) (weaker).
    - Hubble's 2.4 m mirror: this site's history book, chapter 22, section 22.2.

## 12.8 Telescopes working together { #interferometry }

Resolution depends on width, not on area. So two small telescopes far apart, with their light brought together, can
see detail as fine as one telescope as wide as the gap between them. This is an **interferometer**, and the gap is the
**baseline**.

- **Mount Wilson, 1920.** Albert Michelson and Francis Pease built the first such instrument on the 100-inch (2.5 m)
  telescope at Mount Wilson in California. In December 1920 they measured the width of the bright red star
  **Betelgeuse**, the first time any star's width had been measured: about 380 million km, some 300 times the Sun and
  roughly the size of the orbit of Mars.
- **Separate telescopes.** In 1974 Johnson, Betz and Townes linked separate telescopes in the infrared, and in 1975
  Labeyrie did it with visible light.
- **Today.** Europe's **Very Large Telescope** in Chile was designed so that its telescopes can also work as one
  interferometer.

Radio astronomers have joined dishes across whole continents in the same way (chapter 17).

??? note "Sources"
    - The Michelson interferometer on the 100-inch at Mount Wilson, Michelson and Pease, Betelgeuse in December 1920,
      about 380 million km, the size of Mars's orbit, 300 times the Sun, the first star measured: Wikipedia,
      [Michelson stellar interferometer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson_stellar_interferometer) (weaker).
    - The baseline, Johnson, Betz and Townes in 1974, Labeyrie in 1975, and the VLT designed to work as an
      interferometer: Wikipedia,
      [Astronomical interferometer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_interferometer) (weaker).

## 12.9 How much can we see on Mars? { #mars }

**From Earth.** At its closest, Mars is 54.6 million km away. On a night of excellent seeing, 0.4″, the finest detail
a large telescope can show on Mars is about 100 km across, the size of a big crater. Hubble, at 0.05″, gets down to
about 13 km. That is why the Mars of the telescope was a world of vague light and dark patches, and why observers
straining at the limit could see "canals" that were not there. In 1909 Eugène Antoniadi, looking through the 83 cm
lens at Meudon near Paris, saw none (history book,
[chapter 17, section 17.8](../history/17-Herschel-and-the-Canals-of-Mars.md#illusion)).

**From orbit.** The HiRISE telescope (chapter 9) has a 0.5 m mirror. For green light its diffraction limit is
$1.22 \times 550\times10^{-9} / 0.5 = 1.3\times10^{-6}$ radians. From 300 km up that is about 0.4 m, and each pixel
of its camera covers about 0.3 m. Being close matters far more than being big.

**From Mars.** Phobos, the larger of Mars's two moons, is about 22 km across and only about 6,000 km above the ground.
From the surface it looks about 4.1′ across (book 1,
[chapter 1](../night-sky/01-Your-First-Clear-Night.md)). An eye that resolves 1′ could just make out patches a little
under 2 km across on it: Phobos would look like a small disc about four times wider than the finest detail the eye
can pick out.

??? note "Sources"
    - The closest distance of Mars: NASA,
      [Mars Fact Sheet](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html).
    - Excellent seeing below 0.4″: Wikipedia, [Astronomical seeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_seeing)
      (weaker); Hubble's 0.05″: Wikipedia,
      [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope) (weaker).
    - Antoniadi at Meudon: this site's history book, chapter 17, section 17.8.
    - HiRISE's diffraction limit, 0.4 m from 300 km, and 1 µrad pixels: the physics lesson
      [Seeing Earth from Mars](https://physics.akadian.ca/topics/waves/level-7/06-seeing-earth-from-mars.html).
    - Phobos's mean radius of 11 km and height of 5,989 km above the surface: Wikipedia,
      [Phobos (moon)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phobos_(moon)) (weaker). Its 4.1′: book 1, chapter 1.
    - The arithmetic is ours.

## 12.10 Working it out { #working }

**The diffraction limit.** In seconds of arc, $\theta = 1.22\,\lambda/D \times 206{,}265$. For green light,
550 nm, that is about $138/D$ with $D$ in millimetres.

| Aperture | Rayleigh, 550 nm | Dawes, $116/D$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eye, 7 mm | 20″ (but the eye manages about 60″) | 17″ |
| 100 mm | 1.4″ | 1.2″ |
| 200 mm | 0.69″ | 0.58″ |
| HiRISE, 0.5 m | 0.28″ | 0.23″ |
| Hubble, 2.4 m | 0.058″ | |
| Keck, 10 m | 0.014″ (seeing allows 0.4 to 1″ without adaptive optics) | |

**From an angle to a size.** A detail of angle $\theta$ seconds of arc at distance $d$ is $d\,\theta / 206{,}265$
across. At 54.6 million km, 0.4″ is $54.6\times10^6 \times 0.4 / 206{,}265 = 106$ km.

| The nearest moon | Mars: Phobos | Earth: the Moon |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Distance from the ground | about 6,000 km | 384,400 km |
| Smallest patch the eye sees (1′) | 1.7 km | 112 km |
| Smallest patch a 100 mm telescope could show (1.4″), with steady air | 40 m | 2.6 km |

Given steady air, a small telescope on Mars could map Phobos in more detail than the best telescope on Earth could map
the Moon before spacecraft.

??? note "Sources"
    - Phobos's height: Wikipedia, [Phobos (moon)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phobos_(moon)) (weaker). The Moon's
      mean distance: NASA, [Moon Fact Sheet](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html).
    - Apertures: this chapter and chapter 9.
    - The arithmetic is ours.

## 12.11 Where 1.22 comes from { #why }

**A slit first.** Think of light arriving straight on at a slit of width $D$, and look at the light leaving at an
angle $\theta$. Split the slit into a top half and a bottom half. Each point in the top half has a partner $D/2$ below
it in the bottom half, and the light from the lower partner travels farther by $(D/2)\sin\theta$. When that extra
distance is half a wavelength, every pair cancels, crest against trough. So the first dark direction is

$$\frac{D}{2}\sin\theta = \frac{\lambda}{2}, \qquad \sin\theta = \frac{\lambda}{D}.$$

**Then a circle.** A round aperture is narrower near its top and bottom than across its middle, so its light spreads
a little more. Adding up the waves from every part of a circle gives the brightness

$$I(\theta) = I_0 \left[\frac{2 J_1(x)}{x}\right]^2, \qquad x = \frac{\pi D \sin\theta}{\lambda},$$

where $J_1$ is a Bessel function, which is zero first at $x = 3.8317$. So the first dark ring is at
$\sin\theta = 3.8317/\pi \times \lambda/D = 1.22\,\lambda/D$. Figure A was drawn from this formula. The next ring is
less than 2% as bright as the centre.

**Seeing as a telescope size.** The **Fried parameter** $r_0$ is the aperture of a perfect telescope whose diffraction
limit equals the seeing. Excellent seeing, 0.4″, matches $r_0$ of about 30 cm, given for 500 nm light:
$1.22 \times 500\times10^{-9} / 0.30 \times 206{,}265 = 0.42″$. Any telescope wider than $r_0$ gathers more light but,
without adaptive optics, shows no finer detail.

??? note "Sources"
    - The Airy pattern in terms of the Bessel function $J_1$, its first zero at 3.8317 and the first dark ring at
      $1.22\lambda/d$: Wikipedia, [Airy disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airy_disk) (weaker).
    - The Fried parameter as the aperture whose diffraction limit equals the seeing, given for 500 nm, and a seeing
      disc below 0.4″ or $r_0$ above 30 cm as excellent: Wikipedia,
      [Astronomical seeing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_seeing) (weaker).
    - The slit argument is standard; the arithmetic is ours.

## Check yourself { #check }

**1.** (beginner) Why can't even a perfect telescope make a point image of a star?

??? note "Answer"
    Light is a wave, and it spreads out (diffracts) as it passes through the aperture. A star becomes a small disc
    with faint rings, the Airy pattern.

**2.** (beginner) Which makes the smaller Airy disc, a 100 mm telescope or a 200 mm one?

??? note "Answer"
    The 200 mm telescope; its disc is half the size.

**3.** (beginner) Why do stars twinkle more than planets?

??? note "Answer"
    Stars are points, so the stirring air shifts all their light at once. Planets are small discs; the light from
    different parts wobbles differently and averages out.

**4.** (intermediate) What is the Rayleigh limit of a 100 mm telescope for green light (550 nm), and what is its Dawes
limit?

??? note "Answer"
    $1.22 \times 550\times10^{-9} / 0.1 = 6.7\times10^{-6}$ rad, or 1.4″. Dawes gives $116/100 = 1.16″$.

**5.** (intermediate) What does adaptive optics do, and why does it sometimes need a laser?

??? note "Answer"
    A sensor measures how the air has bent the light and a computer keeps reshaping a deformable mirror to undo it. It
    needs a fairly bright star to measure; where there is none, a laser lights up sodium atoms about 90 km up to make
    an artificial guide star.

**6.** (intermediate) What went wrong with Hubble's mirror?

??? note "Answer"
    Its outer edge was too flat by about 2,200 nm, giving spherical aberration, because a testing device had been
    assembled wrongly. Corrective optics fitted in 1993 fixed it.

**7.** (advanced) With seeing of 1″, how large is the smallest detail visible on Mars at a distance of 78 million km?

??? note "Answer"
    $78\times10^6 \times 1 / 206{,}265 \approx 380$ km.

**8.** (expert) The Keck telescope, 10 m across, uses adaptive optics at a wavelength of 2.2 µm. What is its
diffraction limit, and what size of detail is that on Mars at 54.6 million km?

??? note "Answer"
    $1.22 \times 2.2\times10^{-6} / 10 = 2.7\times10^{-7}$ rad, or 0.055″, inside the 0.03 to 0.06″ quoted for such
    telescopes. On Mars: $54.6\times10^6 \times 2.7\times10^{-7} \approx 15$ km.

## Summary

- Light diffracts: it spreads as it passes through an opening. Grimaldi named it in Bologna; Young and Fresnel
  explained it with waves.
- A perfect telescope turns a star into the Airy pattern, with its first dark ring at $1.22\lambda/D$.
- Two stars are just resolved at $1.22\lambda/D$ (Rayleigh); Dawes found $116/D$ seconds of arc by testing observers.
- The eye resolves about 1′, coarser than its pupil would allow.
- Seeing, the blur of stirring air, limits ground telescopes to about 0.4 to 1″ whatever their size.
- The steadiest air is on high island peaks, in the Himalayas at Hanle, and just above the ice at Dome C.
- Speckle imaging, lucky imaging and adaptive optics with laser guide stars beat much of the blur.
- Hubble escaped the air, after its mirror, too flat at the edge by about 2,200 nm, was corrected in 1993.
- Interferometers join telescopes to see as sharply as one as wide as their baseline.
- From Earth, Mars shows detail down to about 100 km; HiRISE in orbit sees about 0.3 m.

**Next:** [chapter 13, Telescope designs](13-Telescope-Designs.md), where we meet the different ways of arranging
lenses and mirrors.
